rows.currentScript: In lines 13 and 14 he returns a cardigan whose owner has left. Yet on line 33 his own jumper goes in "the Friday box". On line 47 he says "It won't fit me next year." On line 48 Miss Bhatt looks "longer than the answer needed", so size is not everything. He is giving up next year, so the trials sheet has a space he won't fill.
rows.whyRewrite: The round-5 fault is fixed: the first sentence is now two plain sentences with the contrast kept ('In lines 13 and 14 he returns a cardigan whose owner has left.' / 'Yet on line 33 his own jumper goes in "the Friday box".'). Every citation checks: the leaver's cardigan is across lines 13 and 14, 'the Friday box' is on line 33, 'It won't fit me next year.' is on line 47, 'longer than the answer needed' is on line 48. Quotations are word for word, the 5 sentences run 12, 10, 9, 16 and 16 words, there is no first person, and the key comes only at the end. The key is still the one defensible answer. But the last sentence fails in two ways. (1) Dropping line 38's "September football trials" removed the only thing that ties the trials sheet to next year. 'He is giving up next year, so the trials sheet has a space he won't fill.' now asserts that link: nothing in the script says when the trials are, and the stem does not say either. A child cannot see why giving up next year bears on this sheet. This is the same fault rounds 2 and 3 were refused for, moved one step along. The script also never sends the child to the sheet itself (lines 37 to 39). (2) 'He is giving up next year' reads most naturally as a future event, 'next year he will give up', not as 'giving up ON next year'. Round 4 said 'letting go of next year'; the dropped 'on' changes the meaning. Fix: keep sentences 3 and 4 as they are. Restore the September link and the 'on' in the last step, e.g. 'He is giving up on next year, and the trials on line 38 are in "September".' then 'So the room at the bottom is a space he won't fill.' To stay within 5 sentences, fold sentences 1 and 2 into one that keeps the contrast word, e.g. 'He returns a leaver's cardigan in lines 13 and 14, yet gives his own away.' The fault is in the script, not the question.

history.reason: Six sentences; the form allows 3-5. It also ends by restating the key verbatim ('one Reuben is not going to fill') without saying why the empty space points to him.

history.script: Line 38 says the sheet is for 'September football trials'. Line 39 adds that there is 'plenty of room left at the bottom'. At line 37 Reuben only passes it, on his way to fetch a bin bag. Nothing says he adds his name. The empty room is a place he could take and does not.
history.reason: 'Nothing says he adds his name.' argues from silence. A passage leaves out countless things, and this option's own tag hint tells the child to 'Find the line that proves it'. 'A place he could take and does not' then states something no line says. The script shows only that he walks past now ('passed the noticeboard', line 37). It never supports the key's future 'is not going to fill' (trials in 'September' on line 38, next to his giving away his named jumper because 'It won't fit me next year', line 47). The key is the intended reading of the writer's purpose and no other option is defensible, so the fault is in the script, not the question. Rest the step on 'passed' and on that later evidence, not on what the passage leaves out.

history.script: On line 37 Reuben only "passed the noticeboard" on his way to a bin bag. Line 38 says the sheet is for "September football trials". On line 47 he explains letting his named jumper go: "It won't fit me next year." September trials belong to next year too, and he is already giving up on next year. So the room at the bottom is a space he is not going to fill.
history.reason: Quotations and lines are right ('passed the noticeboard' l.37, 'September football trials' l.38, 'It won't fit me next year.' l.47), and 'September trials belong to next year too' is a fair school-year inference (Ilya's 'When we're in Year Six', l.15). But the step the key rests on, 'he is already giving up on next year', is asserted, not shown: the only evidence cited is a size reason ('won't fit me'), which a child will read as simply outgrowing the jumper. Ground it in lines that show the reason is not the whole story, e.g. he returns even a leaver's cardigan (l.14) yet puts his own named jumper in 'the Friday box' (l.33), and Miss Bhatt 'looked at him for a second or two longer than the answer needed' (l.48). The key remains the one defensible answer; the fault is in the script.

The point of this sentence is the CONTRAST: he keeps a stranger's cardigan to be returned, yet gives away his own jumper. Round 4 marked that with 'but'. The semicolon removes it, so a 9-11-year-old gets two unlinked facts and has to work out the relation alone. That relation is the whole step. The sentence also packs two line references, a possessive on a line number ('line 33's') and lines as the subject that does the returning ('Lines 13 and 14 return') into one semicolon-joined sentence. That is too dense for this age group. Fix: split it into two plain sentences with the contrast word kept, e.g. 'In lines 13 and 14 he returns a cardigan whose owner has left.' / 'Yet on line 33 his own jumper goes in "the Friday box".' To stay within 5 sentences, merge the last two, e.g. 'He is giving up next year, so the trials sheet has a space he will not fill.' The fault is in the script, not the question.
